**August 24, 1931 — A Monday**

You were born into the worst year of the worst economic catastrophe the modern world had seen. Not near it, not approaching it — inside it, at the moment it was grinding toward its floor. The Great Depression of 1931 was not yet a historical term. It was simply the condition of things.

---

**On the exact day you were born, a government fell and was remade**

In London, on August 24, 1931, the Labour government of Ramsay MacDonald collapsed. The Cabinet had fractured over whether to cut unemployment benefits by ten percent — a measure a May Committee report insisted was necessary to restore confidence in the pound. More than half the Cabinet refused. MacDonald went to Buckingham Palace, tendered his resignation, and was immediately asked by King George V to form a new government. By the end of that Monday, MacDonald had agreed: he would lead a National Government — a coalition of Labour, Conservative, and Liberal ministers — that most of his own party would regard as a betrayal.

The Labour Party expelled MacDonald within days. He had been their leader, and now he was leading a government dominated by their opponents. It was one of the most convulsive political crises in twentieth-century British history, and it happened because a global economic catastrophe had made normal politics impossible. Britain's financial system was under acute pressure. Capital was fleeing. The international monetary order that had organized the world economy since the nineteenth century was failing. MacDonald's National Government was an emergency measure, assembled on the day you were born, to try to hold things together.

It would not fully succeed. Britain would abandon the gold standard within four weeks.

---

**Within weeks of your birth, the world's monetary system broke**

On September 21, 1931 — less than a month after you were born — Britain suspended the gold standard that had anchored the pound for over a century. The decision rippled immediately through the global financial system. Country after country followed. The framework that had governed international trade and currency exchange since the Victorian era simply ceased to function. The abandonment of gold is one of the turning points of modern economic history, and it happened in the first weeks of your life, a direct consequence of the crisis that had already made your birthdate so politically volatile.

---

**Three weeks after your birth, Japan invaded Manchuria**

On September 18, 1931, Japanese forces staged an incident on the South Manchuria Railway and used it as a pretext to invade Manchuria, beginning a military expansion that would eventually become the Pacific theater of the Second World War. The League of Nations, the international body created after the First World War to prevent exactly this kind of aggression, issued condemnations and formed commissions. Japan ignored them and eventually withdrew from the League. The lesson taken by other revisionist powers — that the postwar international order would not enforce itself — was not lost. You were three weeks old when the series of events that would eventually produce global war began its first visible chapter.

---

**Germany was two years from catastrophe**

The Germany of August 1931 was a Weimar Republic in open crisis. The Nazi Party had surged from 12 seats to 107 seats in the September 1930 elections — eighteen months before your birth — becoming the second-largest party in the Reichstag. By August 1931, Hitler was a major figure in German politics, though not yet in power. Six million Germans were unemployed. Banks had failed. Street violence between communist and Nazi paramilitaries was routine. The conditions that would bring Hitler to the chancellorship on January 30, 1933 — when you were seventeen months old — were already present and visible.

You were born two years before the Third Reich. By the time you were old enough to form lasting memories, it existed and was consolidating its power.

---

**The Empire State Building was four months old**

The Empire State Building had opened on May 1, 1931 — three months before your birth. It was the tallest structure in the world, a monument to American ambition completed at the precise moment that ambition had been most severely humiliated by the Depression. In 1931, the building was nicknamed the Empty State Building because it could not find enough tenants. The grandeur and the vacancy together are an accurate portrait of the world you arrived in: enormous human achievement shadowed by an economic collapse that made the achievement seem beside the point.

---

**The arc of a lifetime**

You are 95.

Let that number settle for a moment. It spans a distance in time that is almost impossible to compress into a single life, and yet it is yours.

You were a child of eight when Germany invaded Poland in September 1939 and the Second World War began. You were ten when Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and the United States entered the war. You spent your entire childhood in a world at war — rationing, war news, gold stars in neighbors' windows. You were thirteen on D-Day, fourteen when the war ended, old enough to understand what V-E Day and V-J Day meant. The defining catastrophe of the century was the backdrop of your entire childhood.

You were eighteen or nineteen when the Korean War began — draft age. You were thirty-two when Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas. You watched the Civil Rights movement as an adult, not a child — the marches, the legislation, the assassinations of King and Robert Kennedy in 1968. You were thirty-eight years old when men walked on the moon.

You were fifty-eight when the Berlin Wall fell on the night a young couple was likely laboring to bring into the world a child whose birthdate we examined in an earlier report. The Cold War that had defined your entire adult life, that had seemed as permanent as geography, ended while you were approaching sixty.

The internet arrived in your sixties. The smartphone in your seventies. A pandemic in your late eighties.

Thomas Edison — who had been born in 1847, who had invented the phonograph and the practical light bulb, who had created the motion picture camera — died on October 18, 1931, less than two months after your birth. You and Edison were alive at the same time. You have also been alive at the same time as people who have never known a world without the internet.

---

**What kind of world**

The Monday morning of August 24, 1931 was a world held together by systems that were visibly failing. The gold standard was weeks from collapse. The international security order was weeks from its first major breach. The democratic governments of Europe were under pressure from extremist movements that had learned to exploit economic despair. The United States, which had seemed in 1929 like the future made flesh, was watching its banks fail and its farms foreclose.

The people around your cradle had been shaped by the First World War and were about to be shaped by the Second. They had known the Victorian era as living memory. They carried assumptions about empire, about European civilization's permanence, about the basic stability of the international order, that the next decade would destroy completely.

The world they handed you was in the process of breaking. You were present for the breaking, and for everything that was built afterward: the postwar order, the welfare state, the long boom, the space age, the digital age. You have lived in all of it.

Ninety-five years from that Monday in 1931. There is no other unit of measurement adequate to it.
